27. - The time of Sister Anna del Salvatore’s full rehabilitation was approaching, however, and the first step was Monsignor Cecconi’s revocation of the Institute’s eviction from Florence, with the consequent reassessment of the acts attributed to the Servant of God, which were alleged to have occurred while she was Superior of that house (not after her departure). The Archbishop’s acknowledgement therefore concerned first of all Sister Anna del Salvatore herself.

It was therefore a due act of justice, and if the Servant of God had ever coveted honours, what was now acknowledged might have consoled her self-esteem, wounded and torn by a smear campaign that had been believed even by prudent and devout people. But Sister Anna del Salvatore thought only of the glory of God, the good name of her Institute and how much the Mother had suffered.

Concern for the Florence house continued to trouble the Foundress, now convinced of Sister Anna del Salvatore’s complete innocence; in the final analysis she had been defamed by unworthy people and distrusted by the Florentine Curia precisely because she had not yielded to demands, from one side or the other, to change the Rule and Mother Rosa’s directives.

The future Blessed had intervened once more to have the Archbishop’s measure, now being enforced, revoked. She wrote to Monsignor Cecconi:

“I have never been able to persuade myself that Your Excellency would carry out the order given me to leave the Florence House; yet, as the deadline set for carrying out that order now approaches, I consider it my duty to beg you once more to make a further trial of the due submission of myself and my sisters to Your Excellency. Please deign, then, to give me such instructions as in your wisdom you judge suitable for the good running of that House and consistent with the spirit of the Institute itself.”745

Two letters from Mother Rosa, both dated 24 October 1878, mark the end of the persecution and suffering of Sister Anna del Salvatore and of the Foundress herself over the painful Florence affair, which had already caused so much anxiety and pain.

The first letter thanks Monsignor Cecconi for “the immense charity granted”, that is, the revocation of the expulsion order, which, we repeat, also meant the full acquittal of the deposed Superior.746 The other is addressed to the Superior of the house and refers explicitly to the Archbishop’s attitude: he “has forgiven and withdrawn the sentence, and declares himself a Father in all our needs”, and wished to receive her for a report on the house (“meaning external matters such as the schools and the girls”). Sister Anna Santina was to do this at once, inviting the prelate to visit and bless the community, after which a triduum of thanksgiving to Saint Anne was to be held.747

Having obtained her “rehabilitation”, Sister Anna del Salvatore left Ferrara and returned to the office of superior.

This time her destination was Rome, where the Daughters of Saint Anne had taken possession of a twelve-room house at Vicolo Margana 12 under a seven-year lease from 1 February 1877. Here they continued the activities (home nursing and the education of girls) they had begun in two previous buildings (Via della Lungara 46 and Via dei Pettinari 64).

But the new premises soon proved too small for the growing work of the Sisters, and help came from Fr. Antonio Bennicelli of the Ministers of the Sick (Camillians), who had founded and ran the “Pious Refuge House” for “reformed” women in Via dei Riari. The Daughters of Saint Anne would have free use of a house suitable both for continuing their work and for re-educating the “reformed young women”.

The sisters consulted the Mother, who approved Fr. Bennicelli’s plan, and he thanked her; and since on the morning of 15 October the Sisters of Saint Joseph of the Apparition, having heard of the negotiations, left the house without proper notice, that same afternoon the Daughters of Saint Anne were fetched by the ladies of the Pious Union and taken to the refuge to take possession of it, without ever having seen it.

The old monastery kept its original structure, with grilles, no windows onto the street and strict enclosure. The advantage of space for the Sisters and the boarders was cancelled out by the fact that they all had to live in close contact with the “reformed women” until a separate area for the boarders could be prepared.

On Mother Rosa’s orders Sister Anna del Salvatore, appointed Superior of the house, arrived in Rome in the first ten days of November and was glad to find there her sister, Sister Anna Fabiana, and Sisters Anna Agnese Sismondini and Anna Floria Baggiani. Otherwise the situation was a real disaster.

Apart from the loss-making and costly running of the institution and the constant, demanding supervision of the ladies of the Pious Union who oversaw it with Fr. Bennicelli, life among the “reformed women” made it very hard for the Daughters of Saint Anne to carry out their particular mission. Mother Rosa was informed of all this and openly complained to Fr. Bennicelli.748

Meanwhile Sister Anna del Salvatore bore with her usual patience and understanding the dreadful way of life which, as mentioned, made her mission and her sisters’ extremely difficult among those unhappy women, who were more in need of reform than reformed. From that institution in Via dei Riari in Trastevere, Sister Anna del Salvatore wrote to her fellow sister Anna Letizia Sordi, who had stayed in Appignano, asking about her health and that of some other sisters, but asking her not to mention the name of the place where she was.749 She says nothing more about where she lived. For someone with as delicate a conscience as the Servant of God, the experience of this Roman mission was certainly a further test of her strength of character, capable of facing any situation and bearing any suffering. Speaking to the Mother, from whom she never hid anything, Sister Anna del Salvatore said she was ready “to do everything you […] command”, and to keep her fully informed, she wrote on 18 November:

“I would have so very many things to tell you… For now I will only tell you that in this House… they blaspheme, they curse, and in the end they quarrel and even come to blows.”

Then, worried about the dangers she feared for the Mother, she continued:

“My only fear is that you, dear Mother, may have some sorrow to bear; here I have heard things I thought did not even exist… And however careful one is, one cannot cover everything…”750

For her part, the Servant of God renewed her willingness to stay there, while passing on her doubts and observations about the behaviour of the women in her care:

“… I assure you I don’t know how to handle these women… today too I discovered new things… one I considered the most trustworthy, and the Superior too had a good opinion of her, so she told me, and I have discovered she is a thief… because I kept finding things missing, and now I found she had a hiding place where I found so many objects that I would never have believed it…”

so much so that she called for “a firm Superior”, though she reaffirmed her submission.751

Meanwhile changes were suspected; some foreign Sisters had already inspected the house thoroughly, and the Servant of God did not know how to deal with a Director who was almost always absent and at odds with Fr. Bennicelli.

“But what grieves me,” she added in the letter of 21 December 1878, “is that I fear you will have trouble from this house, because in the thirteen or fourteen years this Community has existed they have already changed, that is, sent away, five different kinds of nuns.”752

It was an easy prophecy, for a few months later, on 23 March of the following year, the Sisters left the House for good.

28. - As early as 1875 the Daughters of Saint Anne had been called by the mayor of Sermoneta to take charge of the girls’ primary education, and Mother Rosa had agreed, sending three sisters with their superior, Sister Domenica Marchesini. The school at once won the favour of the population and the local authorities, who, besides an annual salary of 960 lire, provided grain and oil donated by some charitable foundations. Divided into older, younger and middle girls, the three classes had about sixty pupils, while an evening school provided for those who worked in the fields and could not attend lessons in the morning and early afternoon (8.30 to 2.30). Teaching Christian doctrine, serving the parish and another school, for embroidery, completed the work of the Daughters of Saint Anne in Sermoneta.753

After the Roman experience, this assignment proved unexpectedly pleasant and welcome: the people responded to the sisters’ care, and the town authorities and the Bishop of Terracina were pleased with their work. Reporting on the journey, Sister Anna del Salvatore had told the Mother that they had walked the last stretch, from Tre Ponti to their destination, having already spent what little money they had on the train tickets. Nor was the way easy or short: the sisters had to walk six miles, and now the Servant of God felt very tired and asked the Mother to excuse her from rising at a quarter to five. In her humility she found a way to accuse herself of “hidden laziness”, when the real cause was the strain of the journey.754

The theme, not so much of poverty as of the destitution in which the sisters found themselves, recurs later too, mixed with good news about the sisters and the pupils (“the school […] full of girls, it’s a pleasure, both morning and afternoon”);755 the Bishop of Terracina helped the community and ordered the Congregation of Charity to give the sisters money and food,756 but these were slow to arrive,757 while a dispute arose with the Sermoneta municipality over the previous management.758 Clarifications were then needed, and the Servant of God had to inform the school Superintendent that if things went on like this, the sisters, as Mother Rosa had told her to say,759 would give up the post.

On 26 April 1879 she reported to the Foundress as follows:

“A few lines to tell you that today we went straight to the superintendent and told him everything you said to tell him: that if they give us everything we are owed, then we will hold the examinations at the beginning of June, and otherwise we will leave at once. He has taken until tomorrow to reply, and then we will also go to the mayor and give you an answer straight away…”760

The Mother had decided to withdraw the sisters, and reflecting on the behaviour of a qualified teacher sister, the Servant of God wondered “whether it is Saint Anne who no longer wants her Daughters in this town, or whether it is because of the teacher’s rather unpleasant manner”.761 Sister Anna del Salvatore finally announced their departure for early June, despite the insistence of the civil and church authorities. Mother Rosa’s order was carried out: “They objected,” she writes at the end of May, “but we stood firm, saying that we must go.” She was only sorry that the teacher sister “had not wanted to have [the pupils] sit the examinations”, because “she could have held them, and it would have been more to the Institute’s credit; but here too we need patience”.762

Without a moment’s rest the Servant of God was transferred as a nurse to Ovada, where the first Daughters of Saint Anne had been sent in February 1873 to the “Sant’Antonio” hospital. The sisters had also opened a school for girls, “who are a good number, more than 80, and there are also young women of 25-30, almost all Children of Mary, all devoted, receiving Communion every day”, as the Superior wrote, announcing the forthcoming opening of a school for boys.763

So the Servant of God devoted herself to nursing the sick in the hospital; in a letter to the Mother written as soon as she arrived, she showed not only her well-known trust in Blessed Rosa but also her prudence, telling her in confidence of an unpleasant incident in a patient’s home, where the husband had harassed another sister and herself during the night watch. She reserved further details to tell her in person.764

Her stay in Ovada was quite short, as we can infer from the letter to Mother Rosa datable to June 1879 (she had left Sermoneta at the end of May).

We know little else about that stay, but a testimony from Sister Anna Maurina Moise reports what she had learned from Sister Anna Consolata Massimelli, then a patient in the Ovada hospital. In this house, it seems, Sister Anna del Salvatore also served as portress and lived in a room with two windows, one of which looked out onto the hill called the Rocchetta, where the sanctuary of Our Lady of Graces stands.

Facing that sanctuary, the Servant of God spent her nights in prayer, and in the morning her bed was always found untouched.

“Moreover,” Sister Anna Maurina continues, “the Servant of God showed the greatest eagerness to receive Holy Communion, and having to go out in winter, she braved any weather early in the morning, even blizzards and deep snow, in order to receive the Holy Eucharist; this aroused the admiration of her sisters, who saw something extraordinary in her, both in her love of prayer and in her desire for sacrifice.”765

29. - Although Marianna Orsi held important positions in the Institute, both in Liguria and in Tuscany, she never sought advantages or even mere honours for herself; her only longing was to obey her superiors, serve souls and do the Lord’s will at every moment, hidden with Christ in God. Humility was constant in her, both in accepting the harsh trials she underwent and in avoiding, as soon as she could, all prominence and praise. In this spirit the Servant of God made her relations with the Mother, her sisters, the poor and the sick easy and loving, and she never bore any grudge against her detractors; on the contrary, she always regarded the humiliations she suffered as entirely deserved.

Never a defence, never a complaint, though it would have been more than legitimate; she accepted everything that came from authority, in which she saw God’s will, and took all blame upon herself, not for wrong knowingly done, least of all for what she was unjustly accused of, but for not having been able, in her judgement, to foresee and prevent it, or for faults that only her humility and contempt for her own nature made her regard as such, and even magnified. But the truth had made its way, and the Servant of God’s rehabilitation was now complete, so much so that after her experience among the “reformed women” of Rome, among the simple people of Sermoneta and the interlude in Ovada, she was sent to Palermo to start the first House of home nurses in that city.

First as Superior of the new foundation, she later (May 1884) held the office of Provincial Superior of the Communities of Sicily, and until her death she continued to be directly responsible for the first Community she had founded.

In the biography written by Sister Anna Roberta Frati there is a page, quoted here, about the assignment and the reasons for the careful choice of the humble and great sister from Albareto.

“Meanwhile the Foundress,” we read, “observes her behaviour and reflects on what has happened. At such difficult moments Sister Anna del Salvatore has kept an unshakeable serenity; she has shown herself deeply humble; no word betraying resentment or bitterness has passed her lips. All this is the sign of truly uncommon virtue and of a Gospel life lived consistently and continuously. The esteem that had been clouded returns stronger than before and turns into genuine admiration.

It is natural, therefore, that when Rosa Gattorno assigned some sisters to open a house of home nurses in the city of Palermo at the invitation of Mgr. Celesia, the future cardinal, she should choose Sister Anna del Salvatore as superior of the community.”766

*

[…]767.

Processes of change

towards a new socio-cultural order in Sicily

The economic and social conditions of Sicily in the immediate aftermath of Italian Unification are in some respects better known than those of most Italian regions, at least as regards the matters examined by the famous “inquiries” (Sonnino, Bonfandini, Lorenzoni). On the other hand, the very need for these inquiries shows how superficial the knowledge of the island’s real conditions generally was, and how much concern the revolt of 1866 and the general climate of “opposition” on the island had aroused in national public opinion as well as in the government.

In 1866 Sicily had indeed found itself in “the strange situation of a government that enjoyed the sympathy of no current of public opinion”:768 in opposition, for different reasons, were the very few Bourbon legitimists, the republicans and the autonomists, but also the moderate unitarians themselves, who had suffered the process of centralization and “Piedmontization” that in the first period of national unity seemed particularly intolerable. People seemed to know the new State only through its most unpopular forms of presence, such as compulsory military service, heavy taxation and harsh repression, including arbitrary arrests of real or alleged Bourbon sympathizers and republicans; but even more serious was the rebellious opposition of the common people.

Sicily’s unrest was first of all political, stemming from disappointment with the centralized system established with the country’s unification, a centralism that frustrated Sicily’s traditional aspiration to autonomy, made even keener during the Risorgimento by deep anti-Neapolitan and therefore anti-Bourbon feeling.

“In Sicily,” Francesco Ferrara observed in this regard, “the revolution that has taken place and the side to be taken have only one motive: the irresistible desire to be free of Naples. The cries raised and the principles invoked are mere slogans used out of political necessity, which can change from one hour to the next as circumstances change: nationality and unity are really means, not ends.”769

Referring to the events of 1860, Galasso observed that

“the Bourbons were then paying a double price on the island: the one they also paid in Naples, for their inability to satisfy adequately the demands of a public opinion and a society that had slipped beyond their control and their capacity to lead; and the one specific to Sicily, for the island’s never-overcome reluctance to accept the unitary framework of the Sicilian-Neapolitan State, which the dynasty had imposed in 1815 and implemented with a clear Neapolitan predominance over the Sicilians.”770

The widespread evasion of military service can be seen as representative of the rejection of the new institutional order. The introduction of compulsory military service, then lasting three years, caused widespread resentment among the common people: not only was it an innovation introduced by the government of the unified state, but the well-off could escape it by paying a considerable sum to the treasury. The exact number of draft evaders and deserters is not known, but their number, which in 1863 seems to have been around 26,000, greatly contributed both to the spread of the already endemic brigandage and to the already precarious economic situation of many families, who for years lost the support of their absent menfolk.

*

With 1860 the changes in Sicilian society had been mainly political, but they had been grafted onto a process of change in the social and economic structure that had begun in the first decades of the century. National unity had brought no substantial changes in land tenure or in the ways land was farmed and leased, nor had there been any effective transformation of the productive system, which on the whole remained rather backward.

What made it extremely difficult to transform Sicilian agriculture so as to make it competitive in the markets imposed by the country’s economic unification was above all the persistence of backward forms of landholding: alongside the large estates there continued to exist tiny fragmented holdings, the former the result of the substantial failure of the Bourbon government’s anti-feudal policy, the latter, as Cataldo Naro observed, of the “stubborn refusal of the large peasant middle class, the burgisiddi and metateri placed between the day labourers below and the gabelloti above, to let themselves be proletarianized”, of the “stubborn dream of acquiring a small farm”,771 an attitude of which Naro rightly observes that not only the “economic and social reasons but also the cultural ones” should be studied.772

But it was above all the large estates that characterized the island’s agricultural landscape and determined the living conditions of most Sicilian peasants, which Salvioli would describe vividly soon after the Fasci revolt:

“[...] oppressive farming contracts, a rural population concentrated in large villages far from the land it must cultivate, selfishly administered by the local middle class, which starves and fleeces it with the consumption duty, the hearth tax and the livestock tax, and above all with usury; there, unsafe countryside, without water, houses or roads, and poisoned by malaria; there, a crowd of day labourers, sharecroppers, small farmers and petty tenants, almost always propertyless, lucky if they own a house and a mule, in debt, without hope or confidence of escaping from their hell, living on credit all year round, with advances from the owner or tenant on burdensome and often iniquitous terms.”773

This picture might seem too highly coloured were it not confirmed by numerous other testimonies and did it not substantially coincide with the conclusions reached by the inquiries of Sonnino, Lorenzoni and Bonfandini.

The considerable presence of large estates, which even after the end of the feudal legal system had kept their size and character, and often the name of fiefs as well, and above all the survival of a semi-feudal system of farming and social organization, were in the view of all observers and scholars, Sicilian and non-Sicilian, the main reason for the poor development of Sicilian agriculture: the island’s economy could not be modernized as long as extensive cultivation prevailed over intensive, with pre-capitalist forms of production. The abolition of feudalism in 1812 had not immediately brought significant changes to Sicilian society, although the free disposal of the former fiefs had accelerated the capitalist modernization of Sicilian agriculture, a process that in Sicily was marked less by innovations in farming than by the proletarianization of many small cultivators. It was on small and medium-sized holdings that the traditional single crop of cereals was slowly replaced by more profitable mixed farming.

The changes brought by the unification of the national market created glaring contradictions in Sicilian society, favouring the growth of some sectors of the economy, from which representatives of the Sicilian entrepreneurial middle class profited, while at the same time impoverishing the peasants tied to the traditional, backward structure of the Sicilian agrarian economy.

Sicily had not undergone the capitalist restructuring that in other regions turned independent craftsmen, small peasant proprietors forced into debt and farm labourers driven off the land into factory workers, with the new human and social problems of gruelling hours, women’s and child labour, the search for decent housing and the disorderly, uncontrolled urbanization that changed the face of many cities in the north of the country. Romeo rightly observed that “industrialism remained too modest for one to speak of a social question on the island, with the related problems of working hours and hygiene, wages and employment, women’s and child labour, etc.”; therefore “discussions on the subject would deal exclusively… with conditions in the industrially more advanced countries, without any reference to Sicily”.774 But this absence of industry and of a social question also meant the lack of any organized social services, which, even without industry, became indispensable in the face of the urbanization and proletarianization of large sections of the population.

*

Little or nothing was done in this period for welfare and hospital services, and it is significant that the famous parliamentary inquiries mentioned above also touch on this subject only marginally; the problem of pauperism and public charity was likewise treated only incidentally in the programmes of both Right and Left. In fact, productivist optimism prevented people from dwelling on the existence of social hardship, for which occasional solutions were sought, but which essentially dismissed the existence of the destitute as anomalous; from there it was a short step to imagining that charity could be done away with and replaced by economic efficiency. The spread of the principles of economic liberalism encouraged an individualistic outlook in economic matters, which led to underestimating the problem of spreading poverty, towards which the authorities’ attitude wavered between fatalistic acceptance and culpable indifference.

“As regards Italy between the nineteenth and twentieth centuries,” Monticone observed, “we face a scarcity not only of historical research but also, and above all, of information and of action by governments and the political class in general on the problem of poverty [...]. Data are lacking, or sought and processed only roughly; state efforts to gather information are sporadic and mostly prompted by emergencies, thus suggesting the image of first aid rather than that of curing the ills.”775

As regards Palermo in particular, the historical accounts of Francesco Brancato and Francesco Renda agree. A picture of the precarious economic conditions of most of Palermo’s inhabitants immediately after 1860 can also be pieced together from the results of a municipal inquiry of 1865:

“Apart from servants with an annual wage and a few other categories, the vast majority of workers lived in a state of constant insecurity that made the line separating them from destitution very thin, so that the poor were not only the 2,000-3,000 living in poorhouses, nor the other 26,000 men officially without an occupation. Alongside the nobles, and often on their alms and those of the many religious orders and charitable foundations of the city, lived a crowd of destitute and underemployed people who had always been the soul of every revolt. Dirty and ragged, they lived in unspeakable overcrowding in the alleys behind the two main thoroughfares, Via Toledo and Via Maqueda, in small damp houses and filthy catodi (ground-floor hovels), which wore down their nerves and made them anaemic and melancholy… A poor harvest or any unfavourable circumstance was enough to reduce even workers to begging. The scene of the distribution of meals at the Capuchin friary was heartbreaking…”776

It should be noted that Palermo’s situation, though in some ways emblematic, was certainly not the most dramatic; testimonies and historical research clearly show the hard living conditions in urban centres throughout Sicily.

Clearly these precarious conditions were a constant threat to public order; General Medici, who from 1868 to 1873 was prefect of Palermo and commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces in Sicily, wrote in a report that the discontent spreading through the island, and above all the capital, should be attributed not to conspiracies or the activity of sects and subversive groups but to the social condition of an urban proletariat deprived of the most basic means of subsistence and therefore ready for outbreaks of rebellion like those of 1866.

A report by the police chief of Palermo dated 3 July 1875 stressed the degraded condition of the great mass of Palermo’s population due to lack of work:

“The Municipality,” writes the police chief, “has indeed made considerable efforts to help the most destitute classes through public works, but these benefit mainly masons, stonecutters and carpenters, so that in general the economic conditions of the lower classes are always very sad. This is shown by the almost total absence of large industries, the scarcity of private work, the high cost of food, unequalled in any other city, the high price of housing, the rags emerging from thousands of catodi, the dejected look of proletarian families, and the neglect in which small children are left in the streets.”777

*

In November 1879 Giovanni Raffaele, mayor of Palermo, at an extraordinary session of the Palermo city council, drew attention to the need to extend public charity:

“I mean,” he said, “charity applied in a Christian way to relieve our suffering fellow men, not the kind that fosters and encourages shameless begging. For the poor man we must support on his unhappy path through life is not so much the one who holds out his hand in the street or knocks at our doors. We shall rather seek him out in those filthy, unknown hovels that are called houses but should be called kennels. There whole families who once held a respectable place in society now languish in hunger, covered only by the shame that keeps them out of sight, lacking even clothes. They cannot and would not dare roam the streets begging, and when ill they cannot bring themselves to go to the hospital.”778

The city administration’s spending on charity rose from 250,000 lire, never exceeded until 1877, to 500,000 lire in 1880 and 732,000 in 1890. These were still entirely inadequate sums, not least because what was really lacking were essential services, from sewers to hospitals, from orphanages to schools.

These analyses by the city authorities led to support for and encouragement of the initiatives of Giacomo Cusmano and other priests and religious men and women who were able to win the esteem and respect of the civil authorities: Christian charity created the conditions for dialogue between local administrators, often openly anticlerical, and the priests and sisters engaged in welfare work. The church authorities constantly denounced the economic and social hardship of large sections of the population; but it was not only Catholics who condemned the prevailing political approach, which neglected measures for the most disadvantaged classes in favour of spending of doubtful usefulness. In 1883 Napoleone Colajanni asked:

“Who in Italy cares about the sewers, the water supply, the streets, the poor man’s proper food, the housing of the majority? The municipalities, perhaps, as is their duty? Other concerns, other thoughts buzz in the heads of our patres conscripti! These trifles, these trivialities neither grand nor aesthetic are beneath them… In Messina there was debate in both scientific and political papers, without the calm and courtesy science demands, on the best way to supply it with water; and the water is still nowhere to be seen. In Palermo there was debate for years about cesspits and the best way to remove from the beautiful Conca d’Oro the terrible source of infection where the sewers discharge. But I believe the debate is still going on, while millions are spent on the monumental Teatro Massimo. Fully fifteen million have been spent on theatres, and about another million will be needed just to roof the first. Meanwhile there is an enormous number of poor! In one public dormitory on 15 August 1881 there were 607, and the mayor acknowledged that at least two more were needed. Between 1 and 15 July 1881 alms were given to about 12,000 poor.”779

*

The very limited spread of schooling may be considered symptomatic: according to the first post-unification statistics there were 2,459,477 illiterates in Sicily. In 1861 illiteracy stood at 83.6% of the male population and 93.9% of the female, averages that forty years later, in 1901, fell to 65.2% for men and 76.6% for women. The differences between the various areas of Sicily are also interesting: in 1861 Palermo had the lowest male illiteracy rate on the island, at 80%, and also the lowest female rate, at 89%, while Girgenti had the highest female illiteracy rate, 97.09%. In 1901 the highest illiteracy rates would be in Caltanissetta and Agrigento, while Palermo continued to reduce its rates among both men and women.780

In fact, as under the pre-unification Bourbon administration, the spread of schooling was closely tied to the financial resources of each municipality; so, just as De Costui’s plans for teacher-training schools had largely remained unrealized, in unified Italy free and compulsory public primary education remained more a hope than a reality, as the 1901 figures show, after forty years of administration by the new national state. The Coppino law, which in July 1877 had made attendance compulsory for the first two years of primary school, had placed on the municipalities the costs of teachers, school premises and all other expenses of implementing the law. The consequences were naturally harmful for the southern regions, where a great many towns could not open schools.781

*

If, as we have said, knowledge of Sicily was scant, knowledge of the condition of the Church, starting with its finances, was far scantier. Corleo had already debunked the supposed landed wealth of the Church, but the myth would last a long time, and only after Gabriele De Rosa pointed out the blunder Gramsci had made concerning the economic condition of the clergy of southern Italy and Sicily782 did a more careful reflection begin on the real economic condition of the southern and Sicilian Church. Stabile rightly spoke in this regard of “a Southern question in church structures too”, caused by the draining of capital to benefit other parts of the country, but above all by the uniformity with which the provisions for liquidating church property were applied. In Sicily, as in most southern regions, the Church’s real estate had not been built up around the parishes, as in the rest of Italy, but mainly around the bishops’ revenues and the property of religious corporations, assets hit hard by the laws suppressing the corporations and the subsequent confiscation of church property. These measures deeply affected the Sicilian Church, both materially and morally, since the Sicilian clergy had generally shown no legitimist or pro-Bourbon leanings and had even looked with sympathy on Garibaldi’s expedition.

According to Francesco Brancato,

“no revolution had been lived in Sicily with so deeply religious a spirit as that of 1860, which counted among its zealous supporters, especially in provincial towns, priests and friars who by their very presence gave it a particular character that, in the movement for Italian unity, clearly distinguished the island from the other regions of the peninsula.”783

The popular “Garibaldian” clergy had openly taken sides and had lived with the Sicilian people the patriotic days that, starting with the Expedition of the Thousand, led to Sicily’s annexation to the Kingdom of Italy; the liberal clergy had adopted an open attitude towards the now inevitable secularization of society, while still being hurt by the anticlericalism that accompanied the dismantling of church property. But, as is well known, hopes and enthusiasm were followed by disillusionment, which would have tragic outcomes at Bronte and many other places on the island; in general, however, the humblest classes were those most attached to the Church.

The effects on the island of the anticlerical policy of the governments of united Italy therefore sharpened, among secular and regular clergy and among the people attached to the Church and its institutions, a disappointment and discontent all the more widespread given the support and participation Garibaldi’s expedition had enjoyed. On the other hand, as Martina observed, the separation of Church and State, a classic principle of liberalism, entailed

“a general secularization of social life, which increasingly tended to disregard all religious inspiration, considering religion an individual and private matter.”784

But, as Sindoni has stressed, what brought about a “Copernican revolution” for the Sicilian Church was above all the law of July 1866 suppressing the religious corporations, not least because “before the suppressions the Sicilian Church was largely structured on a monastic basis and on the religious orders”.785 It hardly needs recalling that the laws dissolving religious corporations and liquidating church property had placed the secular and religious clergy in a precarious position and made them hostile to the unified state; this in itself was a major novelty for Sicilian society, which, never having experienced the Napoleonic period, had lived through an unbroken alliance between political and religious power.

Franco Cardini masterfully summed up this phenomenon, which created cultural hegemonies in our country and risked depriving it of its true identity:

“What actually happened was an attempt… to cut the strong, deep cultural roots of the Italian nation, firmly anchored in the Church and the Catholic tradition. Savoyard authoritarianism, secular schooling and anticlerical patriotism (in its liberal or socialist forms) partly succeeded, at least among those middle classes Gramsci called the ‘capitalist bourgeois class’ and the socio-cultural strata serving and subordinate to them. The plan failed, or had far more limited success, with the subordinate classes, especially the peasants, and made very little impact on the ‘deep’ rural worlds of the South, the North-East and the large islands.”786

For the Sicilian clergy the turning point brought about by the succession of measures depriving them of the particular privileges they had enjoyed in the past was traumatic. It was not only a matter of solving the practical problems caused by the sudden loss of the means to carry out their pastoral work and even to support themselves; it was above all a crisis of identity.

“The clergy,” writes Stabile, “thus found themselves in a society that not only no longer guaranteed the Catholic religion but did not even grant it the advantages of complete freedom: legally, because the State controlled the whole system of church benefices; politically, because, lacking popular support, it distrusted the clergy and kept them under police surveillance.”787

Giuseppe Francica Nava, later archbishop of Catania, vividly recalled the reaction of the Catholic world to the statist and anticlerical wave that had broken over the Sicilian Church:

“The soldiers of Jesus Christ, caught unprepared and stunned by the novelty of events, partly fled in terror and abandoned the field to the invading enemy, partly shut themselves up at home to vent their grief in useless lamentation, and partly, out of cowardice and human respect, went over to the opposite camp, becoming accomplices of the new crucifiers of Jesus Christ in the person of his beloved people and his most chaste spouse, Holy Church.”788

The religious condition of pre-unification Sicilian society was fairly homogeneous: the people’s religiosity and their attachment to the Church’s institutions caused the church authorities no particular concern, either in the old urban centres or in the inland areas where new communities had arisen, thanks also to the intense activity of missionary preachers who, as Naro has pointed out, had passed on a special fervour to the people:

“Despite some major signs of dechristianization, in particular certain Enlightenment tendencies, sometimes openly anti-Christian, especially between the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, Sicilian society as a whole rested in quiet possession of its Christian tradition. In the eighteenth century the priority of pastoral care on the island was no longer the first Christian conquest of the countryside and the inland towns [...]. The rural population generally enjoyed adequate religious care. The building during the eighteenth century, even in the smallest and poorest inland towns, of numerous neighbourhood churches, sometimes richly decorated, and confraternity oratories bears witness to the religious vitality of these people, who had already been reached in no superficial way by Christian catechesis.”789

The obtuse repression that followed the Palermo revolt of 1866 probably marked a watershed for Sicilian Catholics: Catholic consciousness had to face a new reality. The problem was no longer the one common to all Italian and European Catholicism of engaging with “modernity” and “secularization”; now the encounter, or rather the clash, was with a concrete reality hard to live with both spiritually and materially. “Secularization” had put on the uniforms of Piedmontese generals who sent religious into enforced residence, and of the men of the “distant” Piedmontese government who dissolved religious corporations, forbade religious to show their membership of the Church by wearing the habit, allowed the circulation of previously banned publications and encouraged Masonic and secularist propaganda. “Modernization”, for its part, took the form of widespread urban unemployment, heavier taxation and widespread draft evasion, in short a general social malaise that the Church could only attribute to the loss of its guidance over society.

Many clergy had become convinced that the liberal revolution that created the new Italian State was leading to the secularization of society, through an ever greater restriction of the Church’s presence in public life and a consequent dechristianization of the Sicilian people, traditionally devout but swept by rapid changes that could undermine their faith.

“The Church,” Guasco observed, “had built its models and pastoral strategies in the context of a predominantly peasant world, after an initial expansion that had favoured the cities. It had therefore taken on the values and mentality of the peasant world and made its way of being, acting and thinking its own.”790

If this is true for Italy as a whole, it must be even more so for Sicily; faced with the new realities of industrialization and the consequent huge migration from the countryside to the cities, with growing urbanization, the creation of a proletariat in factories and services, the profound change in the rhythms of life and the transformation of traditional values linked to the patriarchal family, the Church

“tried to offer analyses and remedies drawn from its history: it therefore reinforced a paternalistic approach, proposing ethical and religious answers to situations that required much more refined analytical tools.”791

A conservative attitude prevailed, in the strictest sense of the word, since what seemed essential was to preserve the faith and its associated system of values, which risked falling into crisis in the face of new ways of life and the values they produced; the Church saw in

“those changes a risk to religious practice and was concerned above all with that; it was not yet able to offer answers to such changes.”792

*

In fact a kind of “fear of industrialization”, which was essentially fear of “modernity” and “modernization”, is a characteristic feature of Sicilian culture: even liberal culture in Sicily had developed while keeping alive the concern to preserve and safeguard human and religious values, and therefore harboured strong misgivings about the consequences of progress.

In the culture and activity of Sicilian Catholicism in the last decades of the nineteenth century the charitable, relief-oriented mentality of the old confraternities and pre-unification charitable foundations coexisted with the spirit of the new organizations, such as the “Catholic Youth” and the “Opera dei Congressi”. It should be borne in mind that, as already noted, in Sicily one should speak not so much of a labour question as of a social question, or rather of widespread pauperism.

“In nineteenth-century pauperism,” Cataldo Naro rightly observed, “the pauperism of the ancien régime, typical of a feudalized society with a subsistence economy perpetually haunted by the fear of famine and epidemics, merges with the phenomenon of ‘new’ pauperism, brought about by the widening of the market after national unification and the introduction of capitalist processes and relations even into the countryside.”793

During the nineteenth century the Church underwent a radical renewal in its view of and attitude towards poverty and charity:

“For the traditional image of charity as a means of the rich man’s personal salvation, the Church’s magisterium substituted a new conception marked by the values of unity in charity and of association as a legitimate means of influencing and transforming economic and social situations intolerable to the Christian conscience.”794

Faced with the poverty, not only material, of the new urban realities of the late nineteenth century, Cusmano, Di Francia, Lipani and Dusmet listened, bent down to observe the needs of the city dwellers, tried to understand their problems and took up a position not of rejecting the city and modernity but of helping and sharing; like Don Bosco in Turin, Semeraro observed, Cusmano in Palermo, and we would add Di Francia in Messina, Dusmet in Catania and Lipani in Caltanissetta, overcame the attitude of rejection and mistrust towards the “city”, which became “the primary place of their concern, the privileged and priority field of evangelization”, where they sought to

“gather up the uprooted and the lost, offering them, along with food and education, what they needed to cope with the emerging and complex urban reality.”795

This was a recurring issue in the life of the Sicilian Church of the time: in Caltanissetta, as Vacca has documented, the choice between “countryside” and “city” was debated among the Capuchins, who after the dispersal that followed the dissolution of the corporations were trying to return to community life but disagreed on where to build the new friary, clashing, sometimes sharply, over

“the two souls, the two tendencies of the Capuchin friar, namely withdrawal from inhabited areas and settlement in the urban fabric, that is, the Capuchin friar between hermit life and preaching, between contemplation and apostolate.”796

Lipani chose preaching and the apostolate, and his choice of where to return to community life was consistent with this; indeed it was part of a project in which the Capuchin was simultaneously engaged in building the friary and an orphanage for girls, and in the spiritual care of the Third Order and of the Company of the Most Holy Crucifix of the sulphur miners.

*

As is well known, the problem of poverty and relief for the destitute was addressed through a constant dialectic between Church and State, which arose once the various European states became aware of society’s responsibility for poverty. This was also a secular awareness, one of the stages in the formation of the modern state in Europe, and it resulted in the creation of a state welfare system and state control over charitable institutions, which until then had all been founded and run by Catholic bodies. In the nineteenth century the state welfare system was called into question and restricted in the name of the doctrine of liberalism, which did not accept the existence of the poor as a natural product of the economic system and considered the poor responsible, and therefore to blame, for their condition. Maria Teresa Falzone, in a recent study, has stressed how the Church in all European countries, opposing this view, continued its work of relief and the promotion of charity while also developing a cultural effort to keep the values of solidarity alive in society. This historiographical theme has recently been studied more closely in Italy, with contributions that reopen some central questions about the Church’s relations with a strongly secularist State and with a society heading towards a secularization that in some circles, by denying the Church’s public role, meant dechristianization.

In Italy the conflict between State and Church linked to the formation of the unified state had very serious consequences in the field of welfare. Hostility towards the Church resulted not only in the expropriation of church property and widespread hostility towards religious institutions of every kind, but also in the considerable difficulty state institutions and local authorities had in replacing the Church’s “works” in its charitable activity. Another consequence was that, in a sense, the Church was forced to turn in on itself:

“Especially in the first twenty years after unification,” writes Falzone, “the Church lived in a state of siege, feeling isolated from a society it perceived as hostile, particularly among the wealthier classes… Thus the pastoral programmes and initiatives of the bishops and clergy aimed at recovering the faith where it had been lost or was in danger, and at strengthening and purifying it among the people.”797

It hardly needs saying that this work of preserving and recovering the faith should not be underestimated or regarded reductively: without preserving the faith there was no room even for charity, although the conditions in which it had to work certainly forced the Sicilian Church, like that of the other Italian regions, to close ranks and deprived it of the chance to widen, as would happen later, the scope and character of its pastoral action.

“But it was a pastoral approach,” Falzone further observes, “that followed defensive lines, wanting to see the Church’s public role in society recognized and committed to ‘recovering the people’s faith’ amid the ongoing dechristianization. It was a rather static conception of society and the Church, leading to a defensive pastoral style typical of a Church living in an atmosphere of strong opposition, in militant commitment.”798

It is therefore significant that, while intent on defending its own existence, the Church never ceased to defend the values that had inspired its centuries-old presence.

A fundamental aspect of pastoral action in this difficult period of the history of Christian charity in Sicily was the effort to involve the middle class, which first meant overcoming the Risorgimento-style anticlericalism it proclaimed and often practised, out of conviction or convenience, and then drawing it into the Church’s pastoral and charitable work:

“The many welfare initiatives highlighted the Sicilian Church’s response. Mining disasters and natural calamities, cholera epidemics and rampant pauperism did not find the Church deaf; moreover, through the practice of charity it also wanted to invite the middle class to convert, returning to the fold of the Church and above all recognizing its public role in society.”799

It was not an easy task, and we still know little about how this recovery took place in many parts of the island: the most extensive studies, by Cataldo Naro, concern Caltanissetta; we know something about Palermo, Catania and Messina, but much research remains to be done.

It is also interesting to note the dense network of relationships among the priests we have mentioned; ties of collaboration and of human and spiritual friendship between La Lomia, Lipani, Cusmano and Di Francia bear witness to an atmosphere the historian must examine. What research shows, then, as Cataldo Naro has stressed, regarding the church institutions of post-unification Sicily, is

“the extraordinary ability to grapple, from the grassroots and not by virtue of a pre-established strategy, in city and countryside, with the phenomenon of widespread pauperism, which besides accentuating the features of traditional poverty bore the marks of the social damage caused by the capitalist expansion of the market. Through the witness of charity of so many priests… the Sicilian Church regained a renewed capacity to relate to the surrounding society, even while politically and culturally marginalized. It even won the respect and admiration of the civil authorities, who often cooperated in its welfare initiatives.”800

It should also be borne in mind that in welfare matters public institutions had to apply rules that were not always consistent with a Christian conception of charity and care: one need only mention the distinction between the deserving poor and the idle poor, based on the merely physical criterion of capacity for work. But urban pauperism in late nineteenth-century Sicily was linked on the one hand to changing economic cycles, and on the other to the disappearance of the guild ties in the crafts and above all to the loss, for a variety of reasons, of the network of protection and support formerly provided by the patriarchal family.

In Sicily, through a widespread presence in charitable foundations, hospitals, prisons, orphanages and poorhouses, religious influence in the welfare sector continued to make itself felt even after the secularization of charitable foundations, carried out at different times in all European countries. As the generally little-known presence of religious men and women working in the island’s welfare institutions is studied, the continuity of the Catholic presence emerges; it persisted and grew despite the secularization of society and the more or less explicit anticlericalism of the national and local ruling classes.

A brief but significant survey of the Capuchins has established that

“in Palermo one religious has worked since 1860 in the government prisons, one since 1867 at the College of Music, 6 friars since 1867 for the Bread of the Poor, and one since 1888 at the Margarita Institution; at Termini Imerese 5 religious have worked since 1867 at the Civic Hospital; 2 at the Civic Hospital of Marsala since 1870; 2 at the Civic Hospital of Bisacquino since 1869; 2 at the Poor Asylum of Trapani since 1870; 5 at the Palermo Cemetery from 1869; 2 at the municipal cemetery of Trapani since 1878; 2 at the municipal cemetery of Caccamo since 1881; 2 at the cemetery of Ciminna since 1882; 2 at the Poor Asylum of Calatafimi since 1879; 2 at the Caltanissetta Orphanage since 1876; and finally 2 at the Civic Hospital of Palermo.”801

The secularization of charity inevitably brought with it the right to assistance and consequently the criminalization of poverty, partly because the poor classes were considered potentially dangerous; the growing involvement of public administration in welfare stemmed in reality less from philanthropy than from the wish to control the problem of poverty through the powers of law and the courts. The Catholic religion, as Giovanni Gozzini has written,

“shunned the Protestant ethic of individual success through work: in some way poverty continued to belong to the spiritual universe of the virtues and appealed to the remorse, rather than the disapproval, of the rich. The offence of begging thus remained a special offence, in a grey area: prosecutable only when caught in the act, hard to catch in the act, and covered by collusion and paternalism.”802

*

With the transfer of charitable foundations to public control a long and wide-ranging debate also began on the duty to respect the wishes of the original founders of charitable and welfare institutions (what in law would be called “original interests”); once public administration had replaced private benefactors, it was often necessary to transform the old institutions to fit the public role they were now called to play. In this context, far more than the presence of representatives of the original interests, it was the presence of religious men and women that ensured the Christian character of many charitable and welfare institutions.

Martina considered the crisis of vocations that affected all Italy after unification a “clearly positive and beneficial phenomenon”, because with the loss of the material advantages the clerical state had guaranteed, “it eliminated a good part of the self-interested vocations typical of the ancien régime”.803 Zito made a similar point about the marked decline in vocations in Sicily:

“Among the factors that caused the post-unification vocations crisis in Sicily, but undoubtedly helped improve the quality of vocations, are: the secularization of State and society, with the consequent loss of the priest’s social role, previously closely tied to the structures of charity, education and culture; the dismantling of church property and the loss of a whole set of related privileges; and the spread of positivist, secular and liberal culture.”804

The re-establishment of the religious orders also acted in some respects as a selection of vocations. If, as we have said, the dissolution of the corporations profoundly changed the structure of the Sicilian Church, it should also be noted that the re-establishment of community life, at least in some orders, was a time of enormous vitality and proven fidelity.

“Only very slowly and with great effort,” says Naro, “would the regular clergy later recover from the blow of suppression, and in any case they would never again attain the depth and reach of influence they had had before unification. Consequently, from then on the secular clergy would acquire a new and greater importance, bearing almost exclusively the burden of ordinary pastoral care.”805

The situation of the regulars in Sicily exposed them to a series of difficulties, but above all of choices that on the whole confirmed their vocation and dedication to the people, to whom religious men and women had traditionally been close; the massive mobilization of secular and regular clergy in welfare and charity rooted them ever more deeply among the people of both countryside and city, as they shared their faithful’s difficulties, sufferings and hopes. The negative economic effects of national unification, famines, epidemics, mining disasters, the overthrow of the religious orders and the loss of church property, together with the neglect of young people, especially girls, gave rise to an enormous wave of compassion, uniting priests such as Giacomo Cusmano and Nunzio Russo, bishops such as Dusmet and Guarino, and deeply spiritual religious women such as Anna del Salvatore Orsi and Maddalena Morano, who brought about an impressive flowering of charitable works in which education was closely joined to relief.

It might be noted that the new congregations, born of the decline and disappearance of the welfare systems of the ancien régime, could not contain or eradicate the new pauperism arising from urbanization and the abandonment of the countryside, the new forms of urban poverty, especially among workers; but the new congregations of active life arose and worked to relieve, not to solve, society’s ills, and above all to preserve, spread or awaken among the people the spirit of charity, which the public authorities must take up. In this sense it would be reductive, even if it were possible, to analyse and quantify the contribution of the new women’s associations to the fight against poverty and social hardship; far more important was the example and preaching the sisters gave by their choice of life.

It has been observed that Catholics were not equipped to face the “social question” when it arose in Sicily and therefore responded to the emergency with traditional analyses and remedies. More appropriate analyses by the Church and the Catholic world would come later, but it is only fair to stress that no one in those years produced studies or solutions adequate to the situation, which in fact degenerated into endemic revolts and anti-state rebellion and would culminate in the Fasci revolt, but which above all produced widespread poverty, for which the Church, lacking sophisticated analyses, offered “practical service to real poor people, flesh-and-blood people in need of food, clothing, medicine and education”.806

Rather than the inadequacy of the analyses, then, one should stress the continuity of the charitable dimension constitutive of the Church, shown in its care for the neediest at a time when the Church’s public role and the very existence of some religious institutions were strongly contested and hampered by government measures and the dominant culture. On these aspects of social history we should reflect on how weakly the liberal State and Enlightenment and Masonic culture faced the social question, whereas, as Grazia Loparco has recently written, the Gospel message could draw on a centuries-old heritage to place at the service of old and new needs.

“So it happens,” wrote Grazia Loparco, “that the dignity of every person, proclaimed in theory by the Enlightenment but not infrequently evaded in the political and economic choices of the liberal States, is taken up through other channels by women religious. Religious formation points to a brother or sister to be helped and above all redeemed in every needy person, with the difference that, while philanthropy and charity do not undertake to rethink the condition of the poor but only to alleviate their misery temporarily, the sisters commit their whole lives: full time, not holiday charity. And even more they spontaneously work to raise people up from within, since through instruction, education and the development of vocational skills they lay the foundations for a better quality of life, starting with the most practical aspects.”807

*

A fundamental contribution to the social commitment of Catholic organizations in this particular period of the history of the Sicilian Church was made by the congregations of active life that moved to Sicily or were founded on the island, a phenomenon historians have largely neglected or considered marginal compared with other topics of greater interest. The growth of women religious on the island resulted from converging requests both from church authorities, bishops and parish priests, and from civil authorities, mayors and administrators of public charitable institutions; the apostolic value of religious women in caring for the destitute, looking after children in orphanages and nursing the sick at home and in hospitals steadily increased the presence of the new women’s congregations. The periodical La Sicilia Cattolica of April 1894 emphasized:

“While so much has been done in our day to dechristianize and demoralize society by suppressing Monasteries and Convents, it is the work of God that Religious are multiplying and new institutions spreading.”

In Sicily too there was a strong growth of congregations organized on the new model, that is, with simple vows and active life. Falzone has carefully reconstructed808 the birth and development of this intense phase of women’s religious life in Sicily, and her research makes it possible to identify not only the type and characteristics of the new congregations but also when they came into being. Of the eighteen religious congregations founded in Sicily in the nineteenth century, only one was founded in 1856, before the suppression of the corporations; the others arose in the second half of the century, between 1875 and 1897. The founders are interesting too: ten were diocesan priests and two religious, a Capuchin and a Dominican:

“But,” Falzone observes, “almost all the founders are ably supported, in the history of the foundation, by a woman of considerable stature, without whom for the most part they do not undertake the foundation.”809

Most of the late nineteenth-century foundations arose for charitable work: the Servants of the Poor of Giacomo Cusmano, the Franciscans of the Lord of the City of Angelico Lipani, the Daughters of Divine Zeal of Hannibal Mary Di Francia, the Capuchins of the Immaculate of Lourdes of Maria of Jesus Santocanale, the Sisters of the Sacred Heart of Ragusa of Maria Schininà, the Daughters of Mercy and of the Cross of Maria Rosa Zangara, the Capuchins of the Sacred Heart of Francesco Di Francia; in the first decade of the twentieth century, still with the aim of christianizing society through charity, came the Sisters of the House of Work and Prayer of Giovanni Messina, the Franciscans of Saint Clare of Teresa Cortimiglia and the Franciscans of the Immaculate Conception of Lipari of Florenzia Profilio.

This was an original presence, born within the Sicilian Church, which, together with the widespread presence of religious women from other regions, ensured that almost every Sicilian town had sisters. Other congregations founded in the same period, at the initiative of Timoteo Longo, Carmela Prestigiacomo, Giuseppe Guarino and Nunzio Russo, devoted themselves to the apostolate in schools and the related teaching of Christian doctrine. What made the sisters’ work in orphanages effective was above all the new approach, present in different forms in almost all congregations, which combined relief with a comprehensive educational project aimed at preparing those in their care for the world of work. This was a novelty compared with earlier forms of presence of religious institutions, and it was certainly the result of the spread to Sicily of welfare models that had already worked successfully in other Italian regions.

Naturally, founding Catholic schools where teaching followed Christian inspiration was also a deliberate choice to pass on Catholic values and principles, in reaction to rampant anticlericalism and to the plans, pursued more or less openly by Freemasonry, to dechristianize society.810 The educational work of the Catholic congregations was therefore naturally hindered in various ways by the state authorities. According to Acerbi, in the Church’s overall strategy of penetrating the social fabric after the defensive phase, women religious were entrusted with

“the education of young women, that is, of the social factor that would be responsible in the family for handing on the faith and preserving Christian practice.”811

*

Most foundations were made in the cities, confirming the new apostolic climate in which old and new congregations worked, generally oriented to charitable, welfare and educational activities, without of course excluding the pastoral and catechetical aims traditionally pursued by women religious. From the “mainland” there came to Sicily in turn the Daughters of Charity of Saint Vincent de Paul, the Sisters of Charity of Saint Jeanne-Antide Thouret, the Daughters of Saint Anne, the Sisters of the Good Shepherd, the Little Sisters of the Poor, the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians, the Sisters of Saint Anne, the Daughters of Charity of the Most Precious Blood and the Sisters of the Holy Family of Spoleto.

The presence of the Daughters of Saint Anne was particularly widespread: between 1876 and 1899 they opened eighty houses and a novitiate in Sicily. In keeping with the particular aim of their vocation, “to walk towards holiness by identifying with Christ in the mystery of his poverty, in imitation of Mary, Daughter of Saint Anne, and to continue, under the guidance of the holy Mother, her motherly mission in the Church”, Rosa Gattorno’s specific purpose in founding her institute was to serve the sick poor in their homes and to protect and care for girls at risk. Later the Congregation also took up charitable care in hospitals, prisons and asylums and every other form of assistance, education and human and social advancement. Since the work was entirely free, at first the institute’s only income came from begging. The Institute spread rapidly throughout Italy even in the Foundress’s lifetime, and she soon opened houses in Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Peru and East Africa as well. Houses were later opened in France and Spain, so that at Mother Gattorno’s death the congregation numbered 4,000 sisters and 368 houses, 43 of them in America and 7 in Africa.812

The central role of the Daughters of Saint Anne in Sicily has also been rightly stressed by Falzone:

“The Daughters of Saint Anne first came to Sicily in 1876, to Girgenti, where they took over the direction of the Granata Institute, and from there they quickly spread throughout the island. Mother Gattorno herself came several times to visit the many houses on the island. During the nineteenth century they opened no fewer than eighty houses in Sicily,813 though not all survived. Their apostolic fields were mainly hospitals and charitable works in general, mostly institutional. But they were also very active in home services and nursing, especially during cholera epidemics, and in education and schools. An outstanding figure was Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, who also served as provincial superior of the Daughters of Saint Anne in Sicily, but died very soon with a reputation for holiness.”814

Among the effects of this presence, so rich in initiatives and witness, it should be remembered that their way of life gave rise to an exceptional number of vocations:

“The call for vocations at once met a wide response in Sicily, from where the first candidates came, starting in 1881. At first they came from western and central Sicily and, from 1882, from eastern Sicily too. Later, however, young women would come from all the Sicilian provinces. Up to 1900, 175 Sicilian women are recorded as having joined the Daughters of Saint Anne, but this figure is an underestimate. In 1894 a Novitiate was also opened in Sicily, in Palermo, which by 1900 had received 31 young women, while postulants continued to be sent to the other novitiates in Piacenza and Rome.815 It was the parish priests or other trusted persons who presented the young women for admission to the institute. They generally came from the lower-middle or working classes, but there were also young women from the professional or even noble classes. Their age ranged between twenty and thirty, with some younger and some older. Their education did not exceed the usual level of the time, which for girls generally did not go beyond primary school; some were even illiterate, while others already held a teaching ‘diploma’ when they entered. Many, however, obtained it after admission, as Mother Gattorno was very interested in the sisters’ education in view of the teaching role they were to fulfil.816”

The social degradation of Sicily in the last decades of the nineteenth century, especially in urban areas, led the church authorities to make use on the island too of the work of women religious already active in cities in the rest of Italy. Their work was certainly known to the Sicilian diocesan authorities, and it was indeed at the initiative of the bishops most sensitive to social conditions that sisters of various congregations were called to Sicily. Cardinal Guarino, Archbishop of Messina, for example, from 1875 sought help for his welfare works from national congregations with proven experience in caring for the poor: the Sisters of the Good Shepherd, the Daughters of Charity, the Daughters of Saint Anne and the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians thus came to the diocese of Messina, the last to begin a project for the education of girls. Following their example, the “Little Servants of the Holy Family”, later called the “Apostles of the Holy Family”, a congregation founded by Guarino originally to care for sick children and the destitute, also took up teaching.817

It is not easy to determine how far the congregations from regions of Italy where women’s religious life had changed more rapidly influenced the mentality of the Sicilian church world; there must certainly have been a positive influence, not least because the sisters from the “north” had more experience in dealing with urban poverty and marginalization, which in Sicily was certainly a more recent phenomenon; likewise the sisters from other regions had more experience and professional skill in teaching, which only slowly, even in state schools, was being entrusted to women.

The congregations’ aims adapted to social needs, and the church authorities often modified them to meet the most urgent demands.

From the first decades of the nineteenth century charity was no longer expressed mainly through almsgiving but through care and education, which became in some respects “institutionalized, in the sense that they were not regarded as temporary activities that slackened or disappeared once the emergency was over”.818 According to Vittorio De Marco, women’s congregations of active life

“in this contest of charity far outstripped the men’s congregations, and the one founded by Magdalen of Canossa in Verona, the Daughters of Charity, served as a model for many other foundations in the second half of the century too.”819

*

In a society whose social structures and shared values were changing, charitable activity also served to relaunch the Church’s social role; the Church was in no way intimidated by secular philanthropy, which in fact proved incapable of replacing “Christian charity” and ended up being absorbed into the Church’s work of relief and human advancement. In this sense the “works” of this period restored to the Church, which the events of the Risorgimento had put in difficulty, a role in society, partly through bringing the classes closer together in solidarity and seeking social peace, which were the preconditions for restoring a “societas christiana”. In any case it was above all the need to respond to the emergencies created by old and new forms of poverty that produced a wide network of initiatives.

Congregations already active in Italy and Europe, which had therefore already tried out forms of apostolate suited to the new social emergencies, thus came into Sicily, bringing about a less well-known but probably more solid national unification in the sphere of faith and charity. The particular role played by women religious in the second half of the nineteenth century has been highlighted by a scholar especially attentive to the development of women in the life of the Church.

“Experiences,” writes Grazia Loparco, “varied significantly in the pre-unification states and then in the Italian regions; yet in the nineteenth century the image still prevailed of the priest waiting for the faithful in church, even if to offer them elaborate proposals for charitable, economic or devotional associations. The sisters, on the other hand, without open polemical challenge, embodied the Church organizing itself at intermediate levels and going out to meet people where they normally were, and above all in places of old and new hardship, ranging from care to education, from rehabilitation to prevention, from physical to cultural and spiritual destitution, from marginalization to the commodification of the body. In the immediacy of service they, more than the priest, in some respects and in various places, became signs of the salvation they proclaimed, because they spoke a concrete language everyone understood, while church language more often used abstract and ineffective conceptual categories when not combined with the demands of changing lived experience.”820

Loparco’s analysis could in fact cover all the expressions of charity and solidarity of the post-unification Church, in which women religious were in the front line. It is no accident that the apostles of Sicilian charity of this period, Cusmano, Dusmet, Guarino and Lipani, gave women’s congregations of active life a central role in their work of solidarity and redemption among the people of the communities where they worked.

This is another characteristic feature of the new congregations born in the second half of the nineteenth century: they arose not from papal or episcopal initiatives but from the need felt in Christian communities for sisters who could deal with practical problems. And since in Sicily the problems were the same in the various areas where the new active congregations arose, their aims and apostolic activities were fairly similar, generally covering the whole range of charitable, welfare and educational work that characterized religious women in the late nineteenth century. Many of the new congregations began with a specific purpose and a strongly local character, though they later grew larger.

The experiences that matured in the world of charity and welfare are like an underground river running through the whole history of the Sicilian Church, in some respects independent of the vicissitudes of the Catholic movement, though forming the seedbed of the sensibilities that would find expression in the social action of the priests inspired by Leo XIII and later in Luigi Sturzo’s political movement. But the river would continue to flow even after the Popular Party ceased to exist, as we shall see when, during the Second World War and immediately afterwards, the Church and Catholic organizations ensured material as well as spiritual assistance for the people.

The apostles of charity of the late nineteenth century read the signs of the times differently from the social priests who would follow them, but shared with them a realism born of a pastoral outlook that led them to take on their faithful’s needs, without lingering over apocalyptic visions or closing themselves to new things, but rather inventing new and more effective forms of renewed evangelization. The challenges of modernity, which, as we have seen, were widely felt and not only in the Church, were naturally faced and lived with traditional tools, drawing on the Gospel and Christian tradition to keep devotions alive and direct them towards a livelier solidarity with one’s brothers and sisters. In this sense their action should be read as an indispensable bridge between two attitudes, and perhaps two generations: the hardship and isolation that followed the suppression laws were overcome first by closing ranks to defend one’s flock, and later by a political and social commitment aimed at transforming existing social structures.

Borzomati has rightly highlighted how little attention historians have generally paid to the spiritual roots and ideals that guided and sustained the charitable work of the congregations of active life.821 Without knowledge of and reflection on the spiritual choices underlying the readiness to serve the dispossessed, it is impossible to understand their role in unifying the country from this point of view too. A unification brought about, it hardly needs stressing, by the very Church and religious corporations that were regarded as enemies of the unified state.

*

The “municipal question”, as is well known, forced itself on Catholics’ attention and was their first important involvement in political life, partly because of the need to take a direct part in running the charitable bodies and institutions, which were largely the responsibility of the municipal administrations.822 Indeed, it was from the old network of charitable foundations that hospitals arose in Sicily, gradually taking on the character of medical facilities and often changing from refuges into hospitals of a different kind.

Historical research has concentrated on the effects of Leo XIII’s encyclical on both clergy and Catholic laity, prompting priests to leave the sacristies and above all encouraging those who had already made that choice. It is this second aspect that deserves attention in identifying Sicily’s contribution to the reflection that led to the encyclical.

It has also rightly been observed that

“every social encyclical (and others too) is born of action, of presence; in a word, of the Church’s experience. So the encyclical is born of the life of the Church: of the whole Catholic Church living in the world.”823

In Sicily the ground had been well prepared by the social action of the secular clergy and of religious men and women; therefore
