“the encyclical,” writes Eugenio Guccione, “printed in thousands of copies by the Santi Andò press in Palermo, commissioned by the Catholic Lay Society for the free distribution of good books, reached remote places on the island and from then on also represented the most complete summary of the Church’s social doctrine, on which clergy and laity were to base their apostolate.”824

*

Don Gaetano Gabriele’s Funeral Oration contains reflections and judgements on how much the Sicily of the time needed a congregation like the one founded by Mother Rosa and an exemplary leader like Sister Anna del Salvatore.

“One of the many new institutions in which the inexhaustible vitality of the Church is shown is the religious family of the Daughters of Saint Anne, which […] spreads its beneficent influence where the boastful philanthropy of the age does not reach, bringing comfort to every sorrow, balm to every wound, help to every need. Could this devout Institute, then, remain a stranger to our native land?

Making every allowance for the florid style, so far from that of the Servant of God, Don Gaetano Gabriele’s Funeral Oration contains words worth quoting, because they show how Anna del Salvatore responded to the needs of the Church in Palermo and throughout the island.

“[…] Well, the first to set foot in this land of sacred memories and glorious traditions was our Sister Anna del Salvatore, whom the Mother General, Sister Anna Rosa Gattorno, sent to us here as Superior […]. Her virtues soon made her popular and esteemed by people of every class; and although she made a point of concealing and hiding the Lord’s gifts, we soon realized what holiness adorned her and in how many virtues she became our incomparable teacher […]. If she gave splendid proof of Gospel virtues, she made herself most lovable by the foremost virtue of all, humility, which she possessed and practised to a heroic degree.”825

The Palermo house, as mentioned, was the first the Daughters of Saint Anne opened in Sicily for home nursing, but they had been working on the island since 1878 in various educational and welfare institutions: in Girgenti (later Agrigento), Termini Imerese, Aci Sant’Antonio and Aci Catena, while other requests came from elsewhere for similar work for girls.

But although instruction and education were among the main aims of the Daughters of Saint Anne, the Mother had very much at heart the care of her “dear” sick.

A visit to Piacenza by Canon Ignazio Zuccaro, a distinguished prelate of the Palermo Curia, and Don Domenico Bova in September 1879 confirmed these priests in their intention to carry out Mother Rosa’s wish. Since the availability of a house had been made a condition for sending the sisters, on their return the two priests at once set to work to get the project going quickly.826

By 7 October Canon Zuccaro informed the Foundress that he had found a place, rather cramped but suitable for “putting your wish into practice”. It was a small flat on the first floor of the convent of San Marco, just big enough for six sisters, who in any case, as the superior of Termini Imerese, Sister Anna Gaudenzia Martinelli, had assured him, would be content with little. Archbishop Michelangelo Celesia himself, later cardinal, had visited the convent and approved the coming of the Daughters of Saint Anne to Palermo.

Don Bova, for his part, writing to Mother Rosa on 5 February 1880, had promised to provide everything needed for the house and to support six sisters for a year. He kept his word, and about a month later, on 13 March 1880, Monsignor Zuccaro could write to the Foundress: “Everything is done […]; soon nothing will be lacking to receive the longed-for Daughters of Saint Anne.” He himself had “wanted to oversee everything to do it as well as possible, since the excellent priest Bova did not want to appear at all”.827

Three months later the sisters landed in Palermo: Anna del Salvatore, Anna Macrina Paolini, Primitiva Boresi and Paolina Viani, joined by Sister Anna Simpliciana Saviotti, who had come from Termini Imerese to the capital for medical treatment.828

Used to the hardships of her earlier experiences in places where she had gone to start a work (Florence and the “House for reformed women” in Rome come to mind), the Servant of God could not thank Providence and the benefactors enough for the welcome given to the little community. After the telegram to the Mother announcing their arrival, Sister Anna del Salvatore wrote her a letter in which she said, among other things:

“We were very well received, with such courtesy that I cannot express it; an excellent dinner, all that a delicate stomach could wish; the house is lovely, magnificent beds, refectory, kitchen, parlour, etc.; in a word, we lack nothing; Jesus and the Holy Mother are with us, so rest assured that with your prayers we shall do everything well […]. So don’t worry, my good Mother, we are in a real earthly paradise.”

Don Bova immediately provided the “monthly allowance”, the first of the twelve annual instalments he had undertaken to pay, promising to reimburse the travel expenses, which he did four days later.829 The sisters lost no time and began their work at once: the first person they nursed was the maid of the Princess of Belmonte.

When the Archbishop returned to Palermo the community was presented to him, and Monsignor Celesia, writes Sister Anna del Salvatore, “said many nice things to us and that a very large house will come”; he promised to visit and signed a circular letter to the parish priests announcing the sisters’ arrival and asking them to make them known. The prelate regarded the Institute as his own work, so much did he care about it. Monsignor Zuccaro completed the furnishing of the house, “always sending things: a chest of drawers, a clock, a table, a laundry tub”; then Sister Anna del Salvatore had fourteen crates of cloth collected for the curtains ordered by Don Bova, who was doing other things for the sisters too, together with Mother Vincenzina,830 sister of Fr. Giacomo Cusmano (1834-1888), “Doctor, Priest, Founder, Father of the Poor”. This future Blessed had founded the association of the “Poor Man’s Morsel”, which from humble beginnings soon became “a major church charitable structure, presided over by the Archbishop of Palermo himself, involving the parish clergy, various institutions and many committed laypeople from different social backgrounds”.831

After various vicissitudes, towards the end of 1877 Cusmano had gathered some devout women and formed with them the Congregation of the Sisters of Charity, whose official foundation was set for 23 May 1880. Faced with the grave poverty afflicting the people of Palermo after Garibaldi’s invasion, the injustices suffered by the Church through the suppression of monasteries and convents, and by the people through heavier taxation, to which were added the revolt of 1866, the cholera epidemic and other calamities, Cusmano had drawn up a programme for his Sisters of the Poor with the same spirit and some of the same methods we find in the Rule of the Daughters of Saint Anne. In a letter to Sister Giuseppina Marocco he outlined the profile of the “bocconista”:

“The soul who wishes to devote herself to serving Jesus in his Poor, whatever nobility and comfort she comes from, must descend to the condition of the Poor person who represents Jesus Christ to her; she must give all she has in order to attain the good fortune of serving him; and then she must make the sufferings of the Poor her own, taking every care to relieve them of all their misery, begging, working and striving by every sacrifice to free them from the least suffering; and as long as she can do without something, she must never allow the Poor person to go without it, so that if a shirt, a bed or a plate of soup is lacking, it must never be lacking to the Poor, but to the servant of the Poor.”832

Sister Anna del Salvatore, who with her sisters aimed at precisely this, with a particular charism for the Christian education of young women and the care of the sick, gladly accepted this neighbourliness in the same small convent of San Marco; but later, as we shall see, it was feared that the people of Palermo might confuse the two congregations, both in collecting alms and in discerning and accepting vocations.

As a mark of respect for Fr. Cusmano and Mother Vincenzina, who, though so busy with their own Foundation, had done so much to settle the Daughters of Saint Anne in Palermo, the Servant of God and the sisters attended the clothing of the first six “bocconiste”.

The religious ceremony was followed by a modest reception; indeed the Servant of God mentions “coffee, fruit, sweets and other little things”, which she and her sisters accepted. Afterwards the Servant of God thought she had broken the rule, and at once made amends by humbly confessing it to the Mother.

“And so I did,” the Servant of God writes in great confusion, “and I also promise you, my dear reverend Mother, not to commit such a fault again, always with God’s help. But prostrate at your feet I beg you to watch over me so that I may not have the misfortune of displeasing you, and if you should see that this might happen, I beg you for charity’s sake to remove me at once from this fatal danger.”833

Another time the Servant of God accused herself to the Foundress of a case she found doubtful, prompted by the deference due to Canon Zuccaro, asking Mother Rosa for clear instructions so that in future she could act without breaking the Rule or displeasing her.

We quote some passages from the letter of 15 July 1880, noting how humbly and prudently the Servant of God acted, scrupulous about observing the rule on the one hand, but also careful not to offend people’s sensibilities in a setting new to her, where benefactors had to be kept happy within the limits of what was lawful and proper.

“A few [lines] again to tell you what happened to me today. Here it is: the Reverend Canon Zuccaro came and told me that, since there are three days of great feast in honour of Saint Rosalia, and in this city it is customary to eat sorbets and other pastries out of devotion, if I allowed it he would give them to all of us and at the same time have some himself with us… and I didn’t know what to do, and I let slip a yes, because if I told him I couldn’t allow it I was afraid he would take it badly; and then I was sorry to deprive the sisters of such a nice treat, because he does nothing but talk about the Institute and God, and always tries to have it spread (sic)…

So not only did the canon come, but Fr. Bova came too, and they brought ices and sweets in quantity… and I had to take them to the refectory, because the place is so small there is no other way. So for another time I would like [to know] how I should behave, whether I did wrong or whether another time I should do the same... Because here we have no room and there is no other way, as the parlour is the size of a large table and no more… and however quietly one speaks, the others hear and see… because Fr. Cosmano’s sisters hear everything, so there is no other way. But I would like to know how I should behave if something similar happens for Saint Anne’s feast.”834

For the Patroness’s feast the Palermo sisters had been invited by those of Termini Imerese, but Sister Anna del Salvatore, always deferring to Mother Rosa’s will, was inclined to decline the invitation, also because of the cost of transport.835

The Mother agreed, and Sister Anna del Salvatore, thanking her for “the great kindness you always show”, added:

“As for going to Termini, it was truly a blessing that you did not give us permission, because here we had a lovely feast. Fr. Bova came to say Mass for us in the private chapel and then gave us a beautiful talk, and then sent us ices, and then told us that if the Mother allows it he will take us to Trabia for an outing in the country, so there will be no expense, and the sisters would get a little fresh air, because it would be at Fr. Bova’s own country house… All this will be done if you, reverend Mother, are happy with it and allow it.”836

notes.orsibio-en-fn767: For a better understanding of the Servant of God’s work in Palermo and Sicily, it is considered helpful to draw on the Studio sull’ambiente socio-religioso della Sicilia 1860-1900, with bibliography, written by Prof. Alfredo Li Vecchi, Palermo 2002, at the request of the Postulation. Professor Alfredo Li Vecchi, lecturer in modern history at the University of Palermo, consultant to the Cultural Project of the Italian Church and member of the Committee of the Social Weeks, prepared this study with a keen critical sense, showing a deep knowledge of Sicilian reality in the richness of its culture and the complexity of its problems. Among other significant figures who came to Sicily from the “mainland”, the Professor highlights the Servant of God, who in only five years (1880-1885) of living and serving in this land was able to approach people of every social class with great humanity, winning everyone’s goodwill and leaving in Palermo and throughout Sicily an effective witness to her goodness and holiness.
